lines.text: Volcanic islands in the Indian Ocean, once ruled by rival sultans, then by France, and since by many coups. This is the story of the Comoros.
Long before people, the deep waters here held the coelacanth, a fish thought extinct until one was caught in 1938. More were later found off these islands.
Said Mohamed Djohar, born in 1918, would serve as president in the late eighties and early nineties.
Ahmed Abdallah, born a year later, would declare the islands independent in 1975 and become their first president.
Bob Denard, a French mercenary born in 1929, would take part in no fewer than four coups in the Comoros.
Ali Soilih, born in 1937, would seize power as a revolutionary in 1976, and be killed two years later.
Azali Assoumani, born in 1959, would take power as a soldier in 1999, and later win election as president.
In 1974 the islands voted on their future. Most chose independence, but Mayotte chose to stay with France.
In 1975 the Comoros declared independence, without Mayotte. More than twenty coups and attempts would follow.
And in 2009 a Yemenia airliner crashed into the sea off Grande Comore. Only one passenger, a teenage girl, survived.
Small and often shaken, the Comoros still look out over the ocean that made them.
